idiom_name: Typed tee with a bounded drop-oldest microtask queue (RxJS share()/shareReplay multicast as the library variant)
implementation_notes: TypeScript adds types to a single-threaded event-loop runtime, so there is no thread to push the analyzer onto and every synchronous callback runs on the producer's tick: the canonical wire tap is a hand-rolled generic tee whose forward(msg, primary) calls the primary handler with the original object and pushes a structuredClone deep copy into a bounded queue drained by queueMicrotask, giving copy independence (no live-reference aliasing), out-of-band dispatch (analyzer cost never lands on the producer's stack), an explicit drop-oldest overflow policy with a visible dropped counter, and attach()/detach closures so the tap inserts and removes without touching sender or receiver. Where the flow is already an RxJS pipeline, the equivalent is a multicast to a second subscriber: share() multicasts the source (an alias for multicast(() => new Subject()) + refCount()) so the primary subscriber and the analyzer are two recipients of one hot emission, and shareReplay({bufferSize: N, refCount}) additionally replays to an analyzer that attaches late - but RxJS gives you no per-subscriber queue and no loss policy, so a slow analyzer must be moved off the synchronous dispatch path with observeOn(asyncScheduler), and bufferSize must be finite because it defaults to Infinity. Cold versus hot decides correctness: a plain RxJS Observable is cold (each subscriber owns an independent producer execution), so naively adding a second subscriber to a cold source executes the producer twice (an HTTP tap fires two requests) - share/shareReplay make it hot while subscribers exist, and with refCount a reset tears down and later re-subscribes. structuredClone enforces the copy contract but throws if any part of the payload is non-serializable (functions, class instances with private state), so type the tap channel as a serializable snapshot, e.g. WireTap<SnappyMessage> over Readonly<T> copies. Choose the hand-rolled tee whenever the EIP contract's explicit overflow policy and drop counters are required - neither Subject nor shareReplay counts or drops by policy; choose the RxJS multicast when the tap is an operator in an existing stream and replay-to-late-subscriber is the only buffering needed.
pitfalls: RxJS tap() is NOT a wire tap and the name collision fools agents constantly: the operator returns an 'exact mirror of the source' with no second channel, its handler receives the live object ('you can mutate objects as they pass through the tap operator's handlers'), and any error thrown synchronously in a tap handler is emitted as an error from the returned observable - in-band, aliasing dispatch, the opposite of the pattern's out-of-band copy.

shareReplay buffers without bound: it multicasts through a ReplaySubject whose bufferSize defaults to Infinity (the ReplaySubject constructor default) and 'a successfully completed source will stay cached in the shareReplay'ed observable forever' - a message tap with shareReplay() or shareReplay({bufferSize: Infinity}) retains every payload for the process lifetime, so a wire tap must pass a finite bufferSize.

refCount re-executes cold producers and discards replay history: share() unsubscribes from the source when the last subscriber leaves and new subscribers 'reset' by re-subscribing, and shareReplay with refCount: true makes 'all new subscribers receive value emissions from a new ReplaySubject which in turn will cause a new subscription to the source' - attaching a late analyzer to a cold shared source fires the producer again (a second HTTP request or socket) and the tap silently changes what the primary subscriber sees.

An error terminates the shared stream for everyone: after an error notification 'no further next values' occur (RxJS glossary), and on a shared observable the reset on error forwards 'the error to all subscribers and their subscription will be closed' - one uncaught analyzer bug erroring the tap channel kills the primary flow too, so isolate the tap (catchError on the analyzer branch before subscribing, or a hand-rolled queue where an analyzer throw cannot reach the producer).

Default delivery is synchronous on the single event-loop thread: a Subject 'simply registers the given Observer in a list' and multicasts each next to all of them synchronously, and Node EventEmitter listeners are 'called synchronously' (with MaxListenersExceededWarning past the default 10 per event) - a slow analyzer therefore delays the primary consumer unless you insert observeOn(asyncScheduler) or a bounded microtask-drained queue, and nothing in RxJS or EventEmitter drops by policy or counts losses, so overflow is silent unless you implement it.
